title: Kairox tests a single drone designed for air and water
summary: Kairox tests a single drone designed for air and water
body_markdown:
[Kairox Systems](https://www.kairoxsys.com/) is testing an unmanned vehicle designed to operate in both air and water. Its flagship project, Tempest, is an amphibious drone intended to combine capabilities that ordinarily require separate platforms. The company says tests of the transitions between those environments are still underway.


The Fall 2026 YC startup is addressing a coordination problem as well as a hardware one. Its founders say discussions with military users and maritime researchers repeatedly highlighted the need for separate vehicles, operators and logistics when work crosses the boundary between air and sea. Kairox's proposition is to consolidate some of that burden into one platform.


Tempest is described as a fixed-wing aircraft capable of vertical takeoff and landing and underwater operation. At this stage, those descriptions are the company's account of the program, not independently verified evidence of operational readiness. The launch explicitly places the product in testing and says Kairox is working toward procurement.


[Watch the original Kairox Systems launch video](https://youtu.be/bRnMZDK8ZvY)


That distinction is important when reading the company's visuals. The official website labels its Tempest product illustration as a concept render. Promotional imagery communicates what the team intends to build, but should not be mistaken for a photograph documenting a completed test or an accepted customer delivery.


Kairox was founded by three MIT-trained engineers: CEO Joel Santiago-Baretti, CTO Alex Rice and COO Jorge Cavazos. Santiago-Baretti studied mechanical engineering and previously founded a company building ruggedized computing devices. Rice studied electrical engineering and computer science, with experience at MITRE, NASA, MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Draper. Cavazos studied aerospace engineering and previously worked on spacecraft attitude control at Oligo Space, according to the launch.


The team says it has discussed and validated the concept with prospective end users in the United States and allied militaries. That is different from an awarded contract or completed procurement. The announcement does not name a purchasing customer, disclose production volume or identify a delivery schedule, and it does not provide independently assessed reliability results.


For an early hardware company, moving between a prototype concept, repeatable test performance and a product that an organization can acquire are separate milestones. Kairox's current announcement establishes its intended product category and testing focus, but leaves those later milestones open.


The company's central idea is straightforward: reduce the need to coordinate two different kinds of vehicle by developing one that crosses the boundary. Whether that consolidation delivers practical advantages will depend on testing and evaluation that the public announcement does not yet document. For now, Tempest is a development program with a stated multi-environment goal, rather than a verified fielded capability.
